Canonical text and content-hash ids

Source: R/md-identity.R
md_identity.Rd

Phase 5 (dev/IDENTITY.md §3) identifies every name, address, observation and release by an md5 of what the source wrote, so anyone can recompute an id from the raw file and get the same value on any machine. These functions are the R side of that recipe. Ingest computes the same ids in SQL with the macros md_identity_macros() installs; a test holds the two to identical output.

Usage

md_canon(x)

md_hash_id(tag, ...)

md_name_text_id(name_raw)

md_address_text_id(street, unit, city, state, zip5, zip4)

md_release_id(source, version, partition = NA)

Arguments

x

A character vector (other types are coerced with as.character()).

tag

A recipe tag from md_id_recipes().

...

Fields, each a vector of the same length (or length 1).

name_raw

A name as the source wrote it.

street, unit, city, state, zip5, zip4

Address fields as the source wrote them. A source without a separate unit line passes NA.

source, version, partition

A pinned release. partition is the tax year for a year-partitioned source and NA otherwise.

Value

A character vector.

md_canon()

The only change made to a field before hashing:

  1. NA / NULL becomes "".

  2. Unicode NFC, so a precomposed and a decomposed accent are one string.

  3. Every run of control characters, spaces and no-break spaces (\\x01-\\x20, \\x7f, \\x{a0}) becomes one space. Tabs and newlines are whitespace in the data; the other control characters are noise, and folding them in means the field separator \\x1f can never occur inside a canonical field.

  4. Leading and trailing spaces are dropped.

There is no case folding and no punctuation stripping: the canonical string is what the source wrote, apart from whitespace. Matching on case-insensitive keys is the normalizer's job, in the derived columns.

The recipe

id = md5(tag \\x1f canon(field_1) \\x1f canon(field_2) ...), as 32 lowercase hex characters. The tag names the recipe and its version (md_id_recipes()). Changing what goes into an id means a new tag, never an edit to an old one.

Ids are kept as hex strings, not integers: DuckDB's R client converts HUGEINT to double by default, which would silently destroy a 128-bit id.
